chapters.title: Chapter 5: Running a Clean Cap Table in India

lessons.title: Recording Every Change: Allotments, Transfers and MCA Filings

children.text: Three weeks into Series C diligence, the investor's lawyer sends a one-line email: the company's annual return shows 34,487 shares, the cap table shows 35,071, and nobody can explain the difference. It turns out to be an allotment made two years ago where the return was filed late and one entry was never corrected. The round does not die, but it slips by six weeks and costs several lakh in professional fees. Your cap table is only as real as the statutory records behind it.

body.text: Your cap table is a spreadsheet you maintain. The register of members is the legal record of who owns your company. When the two disagree, the spreadsheet is wrong and the deal stops.

children.text: The Records the Law Actually Recognises

markDefs.definition: The statutory register a company must maintain listing every member, the shares they hold and the dates on which they became or ceased to be a member. It is the primary legal record of share ownership.

children.text: Four things make ownership official in an Indian private company: the

, the share certificates issued to each holder, the board and shareholder resolutions authorising each change, and the filings made with the Registrar of Companies. A cap table is a convenience built on top of those four. Investors verify the four, not your spreadsheet.

cells: Who owns how many shares, and since when

children.text: Issuing New Shares: The Sequence That Cannot Be Rearranged

A funding round is not complete when the money lands. Private placements run under Section 42 of the Companies Act, 2013 and preferential allotments under Section 62(1)(c), and both prescribe an order of events. Doing them out of order is one of the most common compliance findings in Indian startup diligence.

body.title: From term sheet to a properly recorded allotment

events.title: Valuation and approvals
events.description: Obtain the valuation report required for the issue, pass the board resolution and the shareholder resolution authorising the offer, and check that authorised capital is sufficient.

events.title: Offer letter
events.description: Issue the private placement offer letter in the prescribed form to identified persons, and maintain the record of those persons. The offer cannot be advertised or made to the public.

events.title: Money into a separate account
events.description: Subscription money must arrive through banking channels into a separate bank account. Cash is not permitted, and the money cannot be used until the allotment is filed.

events.title: Allot within the prescribed period
events.description: Shares must be allotted within 60 days of receiving the money. If not, the money must be refunded within 15 days, after which interest becomes payable.

events.title: File the return of allotment
events.description: Form PAS-3 is filed with the Registrar of Companies within 30 days of allotment. Only after this can the company use the subscription money.

events.title: Certificates and registers
events.description: Issue share certificates within two months of allotment with stamp duty paid, and update the register of members the same week.

body.text: The rule founders break most often is spending the money before Form PAS-3 is filed. The round has closed, the bank balance is real, and salaries are due. Spending it early is a breach that surfaces in the next diligence and is expensive to regularise. Treat the PAS-3 filing, not the bank credit, as the moment the round is done.

children.text: Every Event, Its Form and Its Deadline

body.caption: Cap table events and the filings they trigger

cells: Form PAS-3, the return of allotment
Special resolution, such as a preferential allotment
Within 30 days of passing the resolution
Form SH-4 transfer deed, board approval, register updated
The instrument is delivered to the company within 60 days of execution
Creation of a charge, as with venture debt
Annual return in Form MGT-7 or MGT-7A
Within 60 days of the annual general meeting

body.text: Two India-specific items catch growing startups. Foreign investment brings its own reporting under FEMA, separate from and in addition to the MCA filings, with its own deadlines and its own penalties for delay. And private companies other than small companies are required to hold and issue securities in dematerialised form, which changes how allotments and transfers are processed. Both are worth a conversation with your company secretary well before you need them, since the thresholds and timelines have been amended more than once.

body.label: Late filings are not free
body.context: Most MCA forms attract additional fees that rise with the length of the delay, and some defaults carry penalties on the company and its officers. The real cost is usually the diligence finding, because an investor reads a pattern of late filings as a sign that other things are not being minded either.

children.text: The Reconciliation That Saves Your Next Round

Once a quarter, put three documents side by side: your cap table, your register of members, and your last annual return. Every share must appear in all three with the same holder and the same count. Here is what a clean reconciliation looks like for TiffinBox after the Series B, and the sort of mismatch that stops a round.

body.caption: Quarterly reconciliation, TiffinBox after the Series B

cells: Not yet in the annual return
Expected, the round closed after the return date
Correct, options are not shares until exercised
Reconciles once the Series B is added

children.text: The two lines that look like mismatches are not. The option pool belongs on the cap table and nowhere else until options are exercised, and the annual return is simply a snapshot taken before the Series B closed. What you never want is a difference you cannot explain in one sentence with a document attached.

body.title: What diligence feels like, either way

columns.label: Clean records
points: One reconciled cap table with dated versions
Every allotment supported by resolutions, PAS-3 and certificates
Transfer deeds and the register updated on the day
Diligence questions answered in hours, not weeks

columns.label: Messy records
points: Several versions of the cap table, none of them signed off
Allotments with missing resolutions or late filings
Weeks of remediation, higher legal fees and a nervous investor

body.label: MCA portal
body.description: File company forms, check your own company's master data and filing history, and view what any investor doing diligence on you can already see.

body.title: The allotment clock
body.prompt: Under the private placement rules, within how many days of receiving subscription money must a company allot the shares, failing which the money must be refunded?
body.explanation: Allotment must be made within 60 days of receipt of the money. If it is not, the money must be refunded within 15 days of that period ending, and interest becomes payable if the refund is late. Separately, Form PAS-3 must be filed within 30 days of allotment, and the money cannot be used before that filing.

body.title: Name the return
body.textWithBlank: The return of allotment filed with the Registrar of Companies within 30 days of issuing new shares is Form ___.
body.explanation: Until PAS-3 is filed, the allotment is not on the public record and the subscription money cannot be used. It is the single most important filing in a funding round.

body.title: Which form does this need?
body.question: A founder sells 600 shares to an existing investor in a secondary sale. Which of these is the correct immediate requirement?
options: Form PAS-3, because the shareholding has changed
A Form SH-4 transfer deed with stamp duty paid, board approval of the transfer, and an update to the register of members
Form SH-7, because the capital structure has changed
No documentation at all, since no new shares were created
body.explanation: PAS-3 is a return of allotment and applies only when new shares are issued. A transfer of existing shares runs on Form SH-4 with stamp duty, board approval and a register update, and it shows up on the public record in the next annual return. SH-7 relates to changes in authorised capital.

body.title: The round that was never finished
body.scenario: You closed a ₹3 crore bridge nine months ago. The money arrived on 12 January, the board approved the allotment on 20 January, and you started paying salaries from the account on 25 January. Your company secretary left in February and the PAS-3 was never filed. Share certificates were not issued. The register of members still shows the pre-bridge position. A Series A investor has just started diligence and asked for your shareholding documents.
body.prompt: What has gone wrong, and what do you do now?
body.modelAnswer:
What has gone wrong:
1. The subscription money was used before Form PAS-3 was filed, which is a breach of the private placement rules.
2. PAS-3 itself was never filed, so the allotment is not on the public record and will attract additional fees for the delay, with potential penalties.
3. Share certificates were not issued within the prescribed two months, and stamp duty has not been paid on them.
4. The register of members is out of date, so the company's own legal record of ownership is wrong.
5. Your cap table therefore disagrees with both the register and the MCA record, which is exactly the finding that stalls a round.

What to do now, in order:
1. Engage a company secretary immediately and give them the full picture rather than the tidy version. Regularisation is routine work for a professional and much harder to do halfway.
2. File the outstanding PAS-3 with the additional fees, and take advice on whether any further application or compounding is needed for the breach.
3. Issue the share certificates with stamp duty paid, and bring the register of members and the minute books up to date.
4. Reconcile the cap table against the corrected register and produce one dated, signed version.
5. Disclose it to the incoming investor yourself, with the remediation plan and dates, before their lawyer finds it. A disclosed and fixed breach is a diligence item. An undisclosed one that surfaces later is a trust problem, and trust problems reprice deals.
6. Put a standing process in place: no funding money is spent until the filing is done, and one person owns the compliance calendar.

body.title: Your quarterly cap table hygiene routine
steps: Reconcile the cap table against the register of members and the last annual return, line by line.
Confirm every allotment in the period has a board resolution, a shareholder resolution where required, and a filed PAS-3.
Confirm share certificates were issued within two months and stamp duty was paid.
Confirm every transfer has a Form SH-4, board approval and a register entry.
Check that authorised capital still covers issued shares plus the full option pool.
Update the option register for every grant, exercise, lapse and forfeiture.
List every outstanding convertible with the shares it would produce, and keep it beside the cap table.
Save a dated, signed version of the reconciled cap table, so diligence starts from one file rather than a folder of drafts.

cards.definition: The statutory register of who holds shares in the company, which is the primary legal record of ownership.
The return of allotment filed within 30 days of issuing new shares. Subscription money cannot be used before it is filed.
The share transfer deed used to transfer existing shares, executed with stamp duty paid.
The notice of alteration of share capital, used when authorised capital is increased.
The filing of certain resolutions, including special resolutions, with the Registrar of Companies.
The annual return showing the company's shareholding position, filed after the annual general meeting.
An offer of securities to identified persons under Section 42 of the Companies Act, 2013, subject to its own procedure and limits.
Holding securities in electronic form, which private companies other than small companies are required to move to.

points: The register of members, share certificates, resolutions and MCA filings are the legal record. The cap table is a spreadsheet built on top of them.

A private placement follows a fixed sequence: approvals, offer letter, money into a separate account through banking channels, allotment within 60 days, PAS-3 within 30 days of allotment, certificates within two months.
Subscription money cannot be used until PAS-3 is filed, and spending it early is the most common founder breach.
New shares need PAS-3, transfers need SH-4 with stamp duty, authorised capital changes need SH-7, and special resolutions need MGT-14.
Options belong on the cap table but not in the register of members until they are exercised.
Foreign investment carries separate FEMA reporting, and non-small private companies must hold securities in dematerialised form.
Reconcile the cap table, the register and the last annual return every quarter, and keep one dated signed version.
If something was missed, regularise it and disclose it before the investor's lawyer finds it.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not legal, tax or investment advice. TiffinBox Foods is fictional and all share counts are illustrative. Forms, timelines, fees, dematerialisation requirements, FEMA reporting obligations and the procedure for private placements and preferential allotments are governed by the Companies Act, 2013, its rules and FEMA regulations, all of which are amended from time to time, and some requirements differ for small companies, startups recognised by DPIIT and companies with foreign investment. Always work with a qualified company secretary or chartered accountant on allotments, transfers and filings.
